transcription.tex: Question 1

A sample of size 6 is taken from a population that is normally distributed with mean 10 and standard deviation 2.\par \textbf{a} Find the probability that the sample mean is greater than 12.\par \textbf{b} State, with a reason, whether your answer is an approximation.

\textbf{a} Write $X\sim\mathrm N(10,2^2)$ for a single observation. For six independent observations, $\mathrm{Var}(\bar X)=\sigma^2/n=2^2/6=2/3$.\par Thus $\bar X\sim\mathrm N(10,2/3)$. By calculator, $P(\bar X>12)=1-P(\bar X<12)=1-0.9928=0.0072$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{b} A sample mean from independent normal observations is itself exactly normal. Only the displayed decimal has been rounded.
Question 3

The lengths of bolts produced by a machine have an unknown distribution with mean 3.03 cm and standard deviation 0.20 cm.\par A sample of 100 bolts is taken.\par \textbf{a} Estimate the probability that the mean length of this sample is less than 3 cm.\par A second sample is taken. The probability that the mean of this sample is less than 3 cm needs to be less than 1%.\par \textbf{b} Find the minimum sample size required.

\textbf{a} Let $L$ be one length. Its distribution is unknown. $\mathrm{Var}(\bar L)=0.2^2/100=0.0004$.\par By the central limit theorem, $\bar L$ is approximately $\mathrm N(3.03,0.0004)$. Hence $P(\bar L<3)\approx\Phi((3-3.03)/0.02)=0.0668$.\par \textbf{b} Let $M$ be the mean of $n$ bolt lengths. Use $M\approx\mathrm N(3.03,0.2^2/n)$ and require $P(M<3)<0.01$.\par Standardising gives $P\!\left(Z<\frac{3-3.03}{0.2/\sqrt n}\right)<0.01$. The lower 1% point is $-2.3263$.\par Thus $\frac{-0.03\sqrt n}{0.2}<-2.3263$. Multiplying by $-1$ reverses the inequality: $\frac{0.03\sqrt n}{0.2}>2.3263$.\par So $\sqrt n>15.5086\ldots$, giving $n>240.51\ldots$. The smallest whole sample size is $241$.
Question 4

A random variable $X$ has the discrete uniform distribution\par $P(X=x)=\frac15\qquad x=1,2,3,4,5$\par 40 observations are taken from $X$, and their mean $\bar X$ is recorded.\par Find an estimate for $P(\bar X>3.2)$.

$\mu=E(X)=\tfrac15(1+2+3+4+5)=3$.\par $\sigma^2=\mathrm{Var}(X)=\tfrac15(1^2+2^2+3^2+4^2+5^2)-\mu^2=\tfrac{55}{5}-9=2$.\par For 40 independent observations the central limit theorem gives $\bar X\approx\mathrm N(3,2/40)$.\par $P(\bar X>3.2)=1-P(\bar X\le3.2)\approx1-0.8145=0.1855$ (4 d.p.).
Question 7

The random variable $X$ has the probability distribution shown in the table.\par $\begin{array}{c|cccc}x&0&2&3&5\\\hline P(X=x)&0.1&3k&k&0.3\end{array}$\par \textbf{a} Find the value of $k$.\par A random sample of 100 observations of $X$ is taken.\par \textbf{b} Use the central limit theorem to estimate the probability that the mean of these observations is greater than 3.\par \textbf{c} Comment on the accuracy of your estimate.

\textbf{a} Probabilities sum to 1: $0.1+3k+k+0.3=1$. Hence $4k=0.6$ and $k=0.15$.\par \textbf{b} $E(X)=0(0.1)+2(3\times0.15)+3(0.15)+5(0.3)=2.85$.\par $\mathrm{Var}(X)=4(0.45)+9(0.15)+25(0.3)-2.85^2=10.65-8.1225=2.5275$.\par For $n=100$, $\mathrm{Var}(\bar X)=2.5275/100=0.025275$. By the central limit theorem, $\bar X\approx\mathrm N(2.85,0.025275)$.\par By calculator, $P(\bar X>3)\approx1-0.8273=0.1727$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{c} This is an approximation. The large random sample of 100 makes the normal approximation to the sample mean reasonable.
Question 9

The annual salaries of employees at a large company have an unknown distribution with mean £28 500 and standard deviation £6800.\par A random sample of 5 members of the senior management team is taken.\par A researcher suggests that $\mathrm N\!\left(28\,500,\frac{6800^2}{5}\right)$ could be used to model the distribution of the sample mean.\par \textbf{a} Give a reason why this is unlikely to be a good model.\par A second random sample of 15 employees from the whole company is taken.\par \textbf{b} Estimate the probability that the mean annual salary of these employees is:\par (i) less than £25 000\par (ii) between £25 000 and £30 000.\par \textbf{c} Comment on the accuracy of your estimate.

\textbf{a} The sample is restricted to senior managers, whose salaries need not have the same mean or spread as all employees. Salaries are also unlikely to be symmetric. Five observations give little justification for a normal approximation.\par \textbf{b} Let $X$ be one employee's salary. For the random sample from the whole company use $\bar X\approx\mathrm N(28500,6800^2/15)$ by the central limit theorem.\par (i) $P(\bar X<25000)\approx\Phi\!\left(\frac{25000-28500}{6800/\sqrt{15}}\right)=0.0231$.\par (ii) $P(25000<\bar X<30000)\approx P(\bar X<30000)-P(\bar X<25000)$.\par This gives $0.80354-0.02311=0.7804$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{c} Only 15 employees were sampled. Since salaries are likely to be skewed, the distribution of their mean may still differ appreciably from the normal model.
Question 10

An electrical company repairs very large numbers of television sets and wishes to estimate the mean time taken to repair a particular fault. It is known from previous research that the standard deviation of the time taken to repair this particular fault is 2.5 minutes.\par The manager wishes to ensure that the probability that the estimate differs from the true mean by less than 30 seconds is 0.95.\par Find how large a sample is required.

Let $T$ be a repair time in minutes. Under the normal model, $T\sim\mathrm N(\mu,2.5^2)$ and $\bar T\sim\mathrm N(\mu,2.5^2/n)$.\par Thirty seconds is 0.5 minutes. To have at least 0.95 between $\mu-0.5$ and $\mu+0.5$, each tail must have probability at most 0.025.\par $P(\bar T>\mu+0.5)=P\!\left(Z>\frac{\mu+0.5-\mu}{2.5/\sqrt n}\right)=P\!\left(Z>\frac{\sqrt n}{5}\right)$.\par The tables give $P(Z>1.9600)=0.025$. Thus $\sqrt n/5\ge1.9600$, so $\sqrt n\ge9.8$ and $n\ge96.04$.\par The minimum whole sample size is $97$.

A supermarket manager is trying to model the number of customers that visit her store each day. She observes that, on average, 20 new customers enter the store every minute.\par Calculate the probability that fewer than 15 customers arrive in a given minute.\par Find the probability that in one hour no more than 1150 customers arrive.\par Use the Central Limit Theorem to estimate the probability that in one hour no more than 1150 customers arrive. Compare your answer to part b.
Let \(X\) count customers in a minute. \(X\sim\operatorname{Po}(20)\), so \(P(X<15)=0.1049\).
Let \(T\) count customers in an hour. \(T\sim\operatorname{Po}(60\times20)=\operatorname{Po}(1200)\).\par \(P(T\le1150)\approx0.07589\).

Treat the 60 minutes as independent observations. The observed mean is \(1150/60=19.1666\ldots\).\par Each minute has mean and variance 20. By the central limit theorem, \(\bar X\approx N(20,20/60)\).\par \(P(\bar X\le1150/60)\approx0.0745\), close to the exact probability in (b).
The Statistics Year 2 method approximates the hourly total directly. Take \(Y\sim N(1200,1200)\) and apply the continuity correction, giving \(P(Y<1150.5)\).

transcription.tex: Question 3
A sample of size 20 is taken from a binomial distribution with $n=10$ and $p=0.2$. Estimate the probability that the sample mean does not exceed 2.4.

For one observation, $X\sim\mathrm B(10,0.2)$. Its mean is $np=10(0.2)=2$. Its variance is $np(1-p)=2(0.8)=1.6$.\par For 20 independent observations, $\mathrm{Var}(\bar X)=1.6/20=0.08$. The central limit theorem gives $\bar X\approx\mathrm N(2,0.08)$.\par $P(\bar X\le2.4)\approx\Phi\!\left(\frac{2.4-2}{\sqrt{0.08}}\right)=0.9214$ (4 d.p.).
Question 4

There are 20 children in a class. Each flips a fair coin until they get heads 5 times.\par \textbf{a} Write down the expected number of times each student will have to flip the coin.\par \textbf{b} Find an estimate of the probability that the mean number of flips is at most 9.

\textbf{a} Let $X$ count flips up to and including the fifth head. It has a negative binomial distribution with $r=5$ and $p=0.5$. Hence $E(X)=r/p=5/0.5=10$.\par \textbf{b} $\mathrm{Var}(X)=r(1-p)/p^2=5(0.5)/(0.5)^2=10$.\par For the 20 children the central limit theorem gives $\bar X\approx\mathrm N(10,10/20)=\mathrm N(10,0.5)$.\par $P(\bar X\le9)\approx\Phi\!\left(\frac{9-10}{\sqrt{0.5}}\right)=0.0786$ (4 d.p.).
Question 5

A town is hit by three thunderstorms per month, on average.\par \textbf{a} Find the probability that there are four thunderstorms next month.\par \textbf{b} Use the central limit theorem to estimate the probability that over the course of a year, the average number of thunderstorms each month is at most 2.5.

\textbf{a} Let $X$ count thunderstorms in one month. Using $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(3)$ gives $P(X=4)=e^{-3}3^4/4!=0.1680$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{b} For this Poisson model, $E(X)=\mathrm{Var}(X)=3$. For 12 independent months, $\mathrm{Var}(\bar X)=3/12=0.25$.\par By the central limit theorem, $\bar X\approx\mathrm N(3,0.25)$, so $P(\bar X\le2.5)\approx\Phi((2.5-3)/0.5)=0.1587$.
Question 6

A patient is awaiting a liver transplant. The probability that a randomly selected donor is a match is 0.2.\par \textbf{a} Find the expected number of donors that will have to be tested before finding a match.\par A random sample of 20 patients awaiting liver transplants was selected, and the number of donors tested for each patient before a match was found was recorded.\par \textbf{b} Estimate the probability that the average number of donors to be tested per patient is more than 5.5.

\textbf{a} Let $X$ count donors tested up to and including the first match. $X\sim\mathrm{Geo}(0.2)$, so $E(X)=1/p=1/0.2=5$.\par \textbf{b} $\mathrm{Var}(X)=(1-p)/p^2=0.8/0.2^2=80/4=20$.\par For 20 patients the central limit theorem gives $\bar X\approx\mathrm N(5,20/20)=\mathrm N(5,1)$.\par $P(\bar X>5.5)\approx1-\Phi((5.5-5)/1)=1-0.6915=0.3085$ (4 d.p.).
Question 7

David is selling raffle tickets from door to door to raise money for charity. To reach his daily fundraising goal, he needs to sell 10 tickets. He observes that, on average, an occupant in one in every three houses he visits will buy a ticket.\par \textbf{a} Find the probability that on a given day he reaches his daily goal after visiting exactly 35 houses.\par \textbf{b} In one month, David worked on 20 days, and met his daily goal on each day. Estimate the probability that the average number of houses he visited per day was 35 or fewer.

\textbf{a} Let $X$ count visits up to and including the tenth sale. It has a negative binomial distribution with $r=10$ and $p=1/3$. For $X=35$ there must be nine sales in the first 34 visits and a sale at the 35th.\par $P(X=35)=\binom{34}{9}(1/3)^{10}(2/3)^{25}=0.0352$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{b} $E(X)=r/p=10\times3=30$. $\mathrm{Var}(X)=r(1-p)/p^2=10\times2\times9/3=60$.\par Across 20 days, the central limit theorem gives $\bar X\approx\mathrm N(30,60/20)=\mathrm N(30,3)$.\par $P(\bar X\le35)\approx\Phi((35-30)/\sqrt3)=0.9981$ (4 d.p.).
Question 8

Telephone calls arrive at an exchange at an average rate of two per minute. Over a period of 30 days a telephonist records the number of calls each day that arrive in the five-minute period before her break.\par \textbf{a} Find an approximation for the probability that the total number of calls recorded is more than 350.\par \textbf{b} Estimate the probability that the mean number of calls received in this period each day is less than 9.0.

\textbf{a} Let $C$ count calls in one five-minute period. $C\sim\mathrm{Po}(5\times2)=\mathrm{Po}(10)$. The total for 30 days is $T=30\bar C$.\par By the central limit theorem, $\bar C\approx\mathrm N(10,10/30)$.\par $P(T>350)=P(\bar C>350/30)\approx1-P(Z\le(350/30-10)/\sqrt{10/30})$.\par This gives $1-0.9981=0.0019$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{b} $P(\bar C<9)\approx\Phi((9-10)/\sqrt{10/30})=0.0416$ (4 d.p.).
